sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Foundational Principle 1**: John Morley was the **Secretary of State for India**, and Lord Minto was the **Viceroy of India** during the formulation of these reforms.
• **Foundational Principle 2**: The Act introduced **separate electorates** for Muslims, creating a system where Muslim members could only be elected by Muslim voters, legally institutionalizing communalism.
• **Foundational Principle 3**: For the first time, provision was made for the association of Indians with the **executive councils of the Viceroy and Governors**.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Central Legislative Council size was dramatically increased from **16 to 60 members**, though an official majority was retained at the Centre.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Expanded from 16 to 60 members; retained official majority.
Government control maintained via nominated official members.
Often tested: Did it have a non-official majority? (Answer: No, only provinces had non-official majorities).
Size significantly increased (e.g., Bengal went up to 53). Non-official majority introduced in provinces.
Allowed non-official majority, but many were nominated non-officials, diluting elected weight.
Crucial distinction between Central (official majority) and Provincial (non-official majority) setups.
Satyendra Prasanna Sinha appointed as the first Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council.
Appointed as Law Member following the recommendations of the reforms.
High-frequency Prelims fact: First Indian in Viceroy's Executive Council.

items.definition: A system of representation where specific religious or social communities vote only for candidates belonging to their own community. Introduced specifically for Muslims in 1909.
The Act empowered members to discuss the budget, move resolutions, and ask supplementary questions, enhancing legislative debate scope compared to 1892.
A council composition where the number of non-official members exceeds official members. Introduced in Provincial Legislative Councils but NOT in the Central Legislative Council.
Arundel Committee (whose recommendations formed the background for the Morley-Minto proposals) and the Simla Deputation (1906) led by Aga Khan which demanded separate electorates.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Region / Zone Details**: Provincial legislative councils of major presidencies—Bengal, Madras, Bombay, and United Provinces—saw structural expansions.
• **Driving Advantages**: Decentralization of legislative business and accommodation of regional landlords, chambers of commerce, and municipal bodies into the electoral framework.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Franchise was extremely narrow, discriminatory, and property-based; communal electorates sowed permanent seeds of religious discord.
• **Policy Interventions**: Later superseded by the Montague-Chelmsford Reforms (Government of India Act 1919) which expanded franchise and communal categories.

items.title: Mnemonic for Classification / Sequence
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: 'MINT' (Minto-Morley, Indian Councils, Non-official provincial majority, Terror of separate electorates).
• **Decoded Meaning**: Minto-Morley = 1909; Non-official majority was provincial only; Separate electorates targeted Muslims.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly prevents confusion between central and provincial majorities.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Centre = Official Majority (COM); Provinces = Non-Official Majority (PNM). Lord Minto = Father of Communal Electorate.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently states that the Indian Councils Act 1909 introduced a non-official majority in the Central Legislative Council. This is INCORRECT. The non-official majority was introduced ONLY in Provincial Legislative Councils; the Centre retained a strict official majority.

Mains Value Addition: Quote Maulana Abul Kalam Azad or constitutional historian R. Coupland regarding how the 1909 Act acted as a political watershed that legally codified communal identities, directly linking to the partition trajectory of 1947.

keyTakeaways: The Indian Councils Act 1909 is formally known as the Morley-Minto Reforms, with Morley as Secretary of State and Minto as Viceroy.
It legally introduced 'separate electorates' for Muslims, earning Lord Minto the title of 'Father of Communal Electorate'.
Satyendra Prasanna Sinha became the first Indian to join the Viceroy's Executive Council as Law Member.
